title: Impact of China's WTO Accession on Manufacturing Employment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID).

Why:  
• “Treated” identifies regions with high pre-existing trade exposure.  
• “Post” turns on after 2001, the moment of China’s WTO entry.  
• The interaction treated × post isolates the differential change in employment for highly exposed regions relative to less-exposed regions, netting out common time shocks (year FE) and time-invariant regional factors (region FE).

Key assumption: Parallel trends – absent China’s WTO accession, manufacturing employment in high- and low-exposure regions would have followed the same trend. We will partially probe this with a placebo test (randomly permuting treatment) and an alternative specification that drops the most exposed regions.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)   # fast import / manipulation
library(fixest)       # TWFE estimation with clustered SEs
library(dplyr)
library(broom)        # tidy output

# 1. Read data ---------------------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s34_data.csv"
dat  <- fread(path)

# 2. Basic inspection --------------------------------------------------------
print(head(dat, 3))
cat("\nUnique periods in the sample:", sort(unique(dat$period)), "\n")

# 3. Baseline TWFE DID -------------------------------------------------------
did_base <- feols(
  y ~ treated*post | unit_id + period, 
  data = dat, 
  cluster = "unit_id"      # cluster at regional level
)

cat("\n=== Baseline DID result ===\n")
print(coeftable(did_base)["treated:post", , drop = FALSE])

# 4. Simple DID without FE (sanity check) ------------------------------------
did_simple <- lm(y ~ treated*post, data = dat)
cat("\n=== Simple DID (no FE) ===\n")
print(tidy(did_simple)[4, ])

# 5. Placebo test: randomly reshuffle treatment ------------------------------
set.seed(2024)
dat_placebo <- dat %>% 
  group_by(unit_id) %>% 
  mutate(treated_placebo = sample(treated)) %>% 
  ungroup()

placebo_mod <- feols(
  y ~ treated_placebo*post | unit_id + period, 
  data = dat_placebo, 
  cluster = "unit_id"
)

cat("\n=== Placebo DID (random treatment) ===\n")
print(coeftable(placebo_mod)["treated_placebo:post", , drop = FALSE])

# 6. Robustness: drop top-decile exposure regions ----------------------------
exposure_rank <- dat %>% 
  group_by(unit_id) %>% 
  summarise(exp = mean(treated)) %>% 
  mutate(decile = ntile(exp, 10))

drop_units <- exposure_rank %>% filter(decile == 10) %>% pull(unit_id)

dat_rb <- dat %>% filter(!(unit_id %in% drop_units))

did_rb <- feols(
  y ~ treated*post | unit_id + period, 
  data = dat_rb, 
  cluster = "unit_id"
)

cat("\n=== Robustness DID (dropping most-exposed decile) ===\n")
print(coeftable(did_rb)["treated:post", , drop = FALSE])
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Negative. Regions more exposed to trade should have faced intensified import competition (particularly from China) after WTO accession, lowering manufacturing employment relative to less-exposed regions.

Magnitude: Prior studies find 5–15 % employment reductions in highly exposed U.S. regions; for China the home-country effect is likely smaller but still material. Hence, I expect the coefficient on treated × post (in logs) to be around –0.05 to –0.10, implying a 5–10 % employment decline in high-exposure regions after 2001.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log manufacturing employment before and after 2001 between high and low trade exposure regions.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Regions with higher exposure to trade experienced a positive effect on manufacturing employment following China's WTO accession.
